content: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited eye disorders that lead to the progressive degeneration of retinal photoreceptors, which are the cells responsible for capturing light and enabling vision. This condition results in significant visual impairment and can eventually cause blindness. Symptoms typically appear during childhood or adulthood and include poor night vision (nyctalopia) and a gradual narrowing of peripheral vision (visual field loss). Over time, the loss of peripheral vision progresses and eventually affects central vision. The global prevalence of RP is approximately 1 in 4,000 individuals, with an estimated 100,000 people affected in the United States. Currently, there is no established treatment for RP. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of vitamin A and fish oils, specifically docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), in slowing the progression of RP. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and others, was conducted without restrictions on date or language. The last search was performed on February 7, 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of any age with varying severities and genetic types of RP. Trials that used cluster-randomized or cross-over designs were excluded. The review analyzed data from four trials involving 944 participants aged 4 to 55 years. Two trials focused on individuals with X-linked RP, while the other two included participants with RP of various genetic origins. Among these, two trials assessed the effects of DHA alone, one trial evaluated vitamin A alone, and one trial compared the combination of DHA and vitamin A to vitamin A alone. Two trials were conducted in the United States, while the other two included participants from both the United States and Canada. The trials were generally at low risk of bias. Visual field sensitivity was assessed in four trials. No significant differences in mean values were observed between treatment groups. However, one trial reported that the annual rate of change in visual field sensitivity over four years was more favorable in the DHA group compared to the control group. This was observed in the foveal, macular, peripheral, and total visual field sensitivity measurements. Despite these findings, the certainty of the evidence was rated as very low. Visual acuity, measured on the LogMAR scale, was evaluated in four trials with follow-up periods ranging from four to six years. In one trial involving 208 participants, no difference in visual acuity loss was observed between groups, with both losing 0.7 letters per year on the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) scale. Another trial with 41 participants found no effect of DHA on visual acuity, with a mean difference of −0.01 LogMAR units (equivalent to a one-letter difference between groups). A third trial with 60 participants reported no significant difference in the annual change in the number of letters correctly identified between the DHA and placebo groups. The fourth trial, involving 572 participants, compared vitamin A combined with trace amounts of vitamin E to vitamin A with trace amounts of vitamin E alone. The decline in visual acuity was 1.1 letters per year in the first group and 0.9 letters per year in the second group. Overall, the evidence for visual acuity outcomes was of very low certainty. Electroretinography (ERG) was reported in all four trials. Two trials found no significant differences between the DHA and placebo groups in the annual rates of change in 31 Hz cone ERG amplitude, rod ERG amplitude, or maximal ERG amplitude. Another trial reported a slight advantage for vitamin A in the annual decline of ERG amplitude (6.1% versus 7.1%, P = 0.01). However, the certainty of this evidence was also very low. One trial with 51 participants assessed optical coherence tomography (OCT) and found no significant difference in the constriction of the ellipsoid zone over two years (P = 0.87). The other three trials did not report OCT outcomes. The certainty of the evidence for this outcome was very low. Adverse events were reported in only one trial, where 27 out of 60 participants experienced 42 treatment-related adverse events (22 in the DHA group and 20 in the placebo group). The remaining trials reported no adverse events. No study demonstrated any clear benefit of vitamin supplementation in preventing the progression of visual acuity loss. In conclusion, based on the results of these four studies, it remains uncertain whether vitamin A, DHA, or their combination provides any benefit for individuals with RP. Future research should consider changes in ERG amplitudes and other outcome measures observed in these trials to better understand the potential effects of these treatments.
